title: The Five Superpowers of Consultants (And How to Develop Them)
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Two management consultants argue that the skills that make consultants effective are just as useful to any leader facing ambiguous, high-stakes decisions. They offer the acronym SCALE (Synthesis, Curiosity, Adaptability, Leadership, Engagement) and unpack each superpower with its sub-skills, the problem it addresses and a recommended book. The piece leans on the claim that people overestimate how well they have mastered these skills, and that the gaps show up when the stakes are highest. Leadership is framed as finding an anchor when a room is drifting and absorbing ambiguity without transmitting panic. Engagement is framed as soft power: influence earned without formal authority. It closes with a self-assessment checklist and a promise of deeper follow-up articles, so it works as a framework overview rather than a deep treatment.
points: The SCALE acronym gives leaders a compact checklist of five transferable skills drawn from consulting work.
Synthesis is defined as shaping messy information into insight, which means knowing what to look for and when to stop digging rather than being the fastest analyst.
Sharper rather than more questions is presented as both a thinking tool and a way of building trust with clients.
Leadership under ambiguity means holding productive tension and reframing the decision, as in the board workshop where the question shifted from which option to pick to which risks must be resolved.
Influence without formal power must be rebuilt in every room, so being right is not enough without being relevant and trusted.
quotes: Consultants take large amounts of messy information and shape it into insight that others can act on. We are not talking about simply summarising things. Consultants spot patterns and turn raw data into new insight.
Consultants ask very good questions. Not more, but sharper than most. These are questions that disrupt assumptions and surface tensions that need to be addressed.
Consultants jump between industries, contexts and problem types without missing a beat. They absorb new information quickly and reframe issues in novel ways.
In those moments, what’s needed is a catalyst. Someone who can help the group pause, step back and reframe the challenge. Someone who can absorb ambiguity without transmitting panic.

Consultants rarely own decisions. Their impact comes from earning trust and nudging clients toward better choices - all without formal power. This makes soft power central to the craft: trust, credibility and timing matter as much as logic.
What makes this tricky is that influence must be built and rebuilt every time you walk into the room. It’s not enough to be right: you have to be relevant and attuned to the people in the room.
